analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The estate-tax repeal bill, which drew only one cosponsor, was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and died there without a hearing or vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax — the taxes on passing large fortunes to heirs — for all deaths and transfers after enactment. It was introduced by Rep. Wes Watkins with a single cosponsor, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, and never received any further action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The heirs of the largest estates would gain the most: the bill would eliminate the tax owed when a large fortune is passed at death or given away during life. The very wealthy and their families are essentially the only people the tax touches, since smaller estates fall below the filing threshold. Estate-planning lawyers and wealth advisers would also gain by no longer having a tax to plan around.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes entirely rather than trimming them.
Applies immediately: the repeal covers the estates of anyone dying, and any gifts or generation-skipping transfers made, after the bill is signed into law.
Because the estate tax falls only on large estates, the full value of the repeal flows to wealthy families and their heirs, who would owe nothing on inherited fortunes.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately everyone else who pays taxes. The estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes are a revenue source drawn almost entirely from the largest fortunes; eliminating them would force Congress to either cut programs, raise other taxes, or increase the deficit. The bill contains no replacement revenue.

drawbacks.text: The repeal would erase a major revenue stream with no offset, shifting the cost to other taxpayers or to programs funded by general revenue, since estate and gift taxes are collected almost exclusively from large fortunes.

The estate tax already exempted most estates from any tax at all in the 1990s — only a small fraction of deaths owed it — so the bill's benefit would concentrate in a few thousand of the wealthiest families each year while the cost spread across everyone.

Repeal would make it far easier to pass unlimited wealth across generations untouched, and would also remove the gift tax that prevents the wealthy from dodging income tax by giving assets away during life.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are narrow and enormous in size: a full repeal of taxes that touch only the largest fortunes, delivered immediately to whoever dies or gifts after enactment. The costs are broad: lost federal revenue that someone else has to make up, with no replacement mechanism in the bill. For ordinary working people the bill offers essentially nothing and asks them to share in the fiscal cost; the honest weighing is that this is a wealth transfer to the richest families dressed as tax simplification.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wes Watkins of Oklahoma introduced the Death Tax Repeal Act on March 20, 1997, calling for full repeal of the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor — a single House Republican — over its entire life.
Ways and Means took no further action on the bill, and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, killing the bill with no committee report, no floor vote, and no action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury and ordinary taxpayers are better off because the bill died: the estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes remained in place, so the cost of the repeal never had to be made up through other taxes or program cuts. Concentrated wealth continued to pay the tax that only large estates owe.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: General taxpayers; the estate tax survived

for.name: Rep. Wes Watkins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: One House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's only supporters on the record were its Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the taxes owed on passing large fortunes at death or by gift, a benefit only the biggest estates receive. The revenue those taxes raise would otherwise come from no one but the wealthy, so repeal shifts the burden toward everyone else.

Full repeal would have removed the complex estate, gift, and generation-skipping rules that the estate-planning industry is built to navigate, cutting demand for its services. That loss would have come alongside a genuine windfall to their wealthy clients.
